transcript:
Header: 2025-08-15 14:00 PDT | Duration: 62 mins | Recorder: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Ethan Myers (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood Sec PM); Michael Chen (CISO, Silvergate), Anita Gomez (Cloud Architect), David Ortiz (Head of Infra), Sara Lee (Compliance)

Summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): quick security deep dive focused on private VPC deployment, ingress/egress policy, KMS and audit logs. Some notes about SOC two and ISO, okta SSO, and network peering.

00:00 Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call — if you can just say name and role real quick.
00:06 Michael (Silvergate): Michael Chen, CISO. Hi.
00:09 Anita: Anita Gomez, Cloud Architect.
00:11 David: David Ortiz, infra.
00:13 Sara: Sara Lee, compliance.
00:15 Priya (Redwood): Priya Rao, solutions engineering.
00:18 Ethan: Great, thanks. The goal today is to walk through our Private VPC deployment pattern, how we handle network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, plus encryption and audit considerations for SOC 2/ISO. We'll try to leave time for specific questions.

01:02 Priya: I'll share my screen — quick diagram, high level. So typical deployment starts with a control plane in Redwood-managed env, then a private data plane in the customer's VPC. We support two main topologies: VPC peering and PrivateLink / VPN-based connections. Peering is simpler but has some routing constraints, PrivateLink gives us more control and avoids route table complexity.
01:35 Anita: Sorry to interrupt, can you clarify: in peering we need transitive routing? We won't do transitive for security reasons.
01:40 Priya: Yes, exactly. With peering there's no transitive routing. If you have hub-spoke you'd need a central router. For us, customers often prefer PrivateLink or a dedicated VPC owned by Redwood in the same account with strict IAM.

03:10 Ethan: Quick qualifier — Silvergate's requirement was strict no-public-egress for sensitive workloads, right? Anita, David you mentioned egress control during presales.
03:18 Anita: Correct. Anything that touches PII or transaction data must not egress to public internet except via approved egress points. We also have strict logging and retention rules for audit.
03:27 Sara: And SOC 2 wants evidence of network controls, config change logs, who can modify firewall rules, etc.

04:00 Priya: Ok, so our recommended pattern: private subnets with no IGW, NAT or egress-only gateways only in a monitored subnet if outbound internet required; otherwise use PrivateLink to handshake with Redwood endpoints. For ingress we either use an internal NLB in front of the service or use PrivateLink endpoints — that way there's no public ALB.
04:28 David: How do you handle TLS termination and mTLS? We want mutual TLS between our app and Redwood's inference nodes.
04:34 Priya: We can terminate TLS on the NLB and then do mTLS to the backend; we support client certs and mTLS via our sidecar. For BYOK scenarios, we integrate with your KMS and can use customer-managed keys for data at rest.

06:10 Michael: On KMS/HSM — we need HSM-backed keys, FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 compliant. Can Redwood plug into our HSM or do you manage keys?
06:22 Carlos (Redwood): We support multiple modes: Redwood-managed keys (default), customer-managed keys in cloud KMS (BYOK), and in some on-prem options we can integrate with an HSM via PKCS#11 or KMIP. For SOC 2 customers with stricter needs we recommend BYOK with HSM backing. We also provide key rotation policies and logs for key usage.

07:05 Sara: Is there proof of HSM integration in your compliance pack? We need to show auditors.
07:10 Ethan: Yes, we'll share our security whitepaper and the HSM integration notes. We'll also share our SOC 2 report and ISO certs — I can put them on the secure share after this call.

08:00 Anita: Back to network — what about egress filtering? We want to whitelist destinations for any egress, and block unpredictable DNS/HTTP calls from inference nodes.
08:12 Priya: We typically put an egress proxy in the path or use NAT with strict proxying; you can also route egress through your own egress appliances (firewalls) by setting route tables. We support forcing egress through customer-managed proxies so outbound hosts are known and whitelisted.

09:30 David: How do you handle software updates/patching for the private nodes? We need to see CMDB entries and patch evidence for ISO.
09:38 Carlos: For private deployments, patching can be done either by Redwood (managed node image updates pushed via our orchestration) or by the customer if they prefer self-managed. We keep immutable images and record updates in our deployment logs; we can export those to your SIEM.

11:00 Michael: Audit logging — what do we get? Flow logs, API access logs, admin actions?
11:07 Priya: We emit VPC flow logs (or you can enable them), application logs, and control plane audit logs. For AWS we push CloudTrail-style logs; we can stream logs to your SIEM (e.g., Splunk, Datadog). We also keep an internal audit trail for config changes and RBAC events.
11:30 Sara: Retention? We have 7 years for some records. Can you support long-term retention or archival?
11:36 Carlos: We can export logs to S3/your archive or integrate with your log retention tooling. Redwood's default retention is shorter, but for enterprise customers we offer log export pipelines and long-term storage options.

13:05 Priya: On RBAC and SSO: we integrate with Okta/SAML, support SCIM for user provisioning, and map roles to least-privilege permissions. Admin actions require 2-person approval for certain ops in our control plane if you enable elevated ops guardrails.
13:28 Anita: We need role separation — developers shouldn't be able to change firewall rules.
13:33 Priya: Absolutely, that's standard. We can create separate roles: infra-admin, app-admin, auditor, etc. You can sync groups from Okta and we honor group-to-role mapping.

15:00 David: Network ACLs vs security groups — what do you recommend for host-level controls?
15:07 Priya: Security groups are stateful and easier for host-level allow lists; NACLs are stateless and good for subnet-level deny rules. We recommend defense-in-depth: use security groups to restrict ports between services and NACLs for broad egress deny if needed.

16:30 Michael: Do you support IP allow lists for admin console access? We want to restrict the console to our corporate IPs and the ops VPN.
16:38 Ethan: Yes, we support IP allow-lists for the Redwood console as well as SSO enforcement. For Private deployments you can host the control plane locally and restrict access to your management network.

18:00 Anita: If we use PrivateLink, how is routing configured? Any special peering?
18:07 Priya: With PrivateLink we create an endpoint service in our account. You create an interface endpoint in your VPC that maps to that service — no route table changes or peering, traffic stays on AWS backbone. This reduces attack surface compared to classic peering.
18:25 David: Are there extra costs for PrivateLink vs peering?
18:28 Ethan: Yes, PrivateLink has per-hour/per-GB charges on AWS; we can run cost estimates during the pilot. Many customers choose PrivateLink for security despite cost.

20:00 Michael: Firewalling — do you have recommended port lists and protocols? We need a minimal allow list for inference traffic.
20:07 Priya: Minimal layout: HTTPS (443) to the NLB/PrivateLink endpoint, ephemeral high ports between sidecars and worker processes depending on our runtime; we will give you a concrete port matrix. Admin plane uses SSH only if you enable bastion; otherwise we use SSM-like agents over the private channel.

22:30 Anita: What's your stance on bastions / jump hosts? We prefer no direct SSH from internet.
22:36 Priya: We always recommend bastion hosts in a management subnet, locked down by SG and MFA required. For additional security, we support session recording and require Just-In-Time access.

24:00 David: IDS/IPS — do you integrate with network IDS, or provide host-level detection?
24:08 Carlos: We integrate with common IDS/IPS platforms via mirror or we can push logs to your IDS. Host-level agents for EDR are supported on homed images. We also provide signature alerts for suspicious API calls in the control plane.

26:00 Michael: Data residency — we need all inference nodes to be in us-east-1 and certain data to never leave region. Does Redwood honor per-deployment region pinning?
26:07 Ethan: Yes, deployments are region-pinned. For Private you can choose the region; for Dedicated we can reserve capacity in a region. We also support on-prem for strict residency.

28:30 Sara: One more compliance question — how do you provide attestations for config changes, who signed-off, and evidence for auditors?
28:38 Carlos: We can produce exportable audit trails with timestamps, actor identity (via SSO), and diffs of config change. For control plane changes we include the approval workflow record.

30:00 Priya: Quick demo of example VPC diagram — showing three private subnets: infra, compute, and management. Ingress via PrivateLink into compute. Egress routed to a security appliance cluster in a transit VPC.
30:28 Anita: That transit VPC is owned by who?
30:31 Priya: Usually customer-owned; Redwood can also host it if required but most customers run a central transit VPC for centralized egress/firewalling.

32:00 David: What about health checks and service discovery — do those open more ports?
32:07 Priya: Health checks are internal only; we keep them on private ports and do not expose health endpoints to public. Service discovery uses internal DNS only.

34:00 Michael: On logging integration — can you push to our Splunk via VPC peering?
34:07 Priya: Yes, we can forward logs via a private endpoint to your logging stack. Alternatively, we can drop logs to a customer S3 and you ingest. We support encrypted transport and sign logs with keys for non-repudiation.

36:00 Sara: For SOC 2 we need to show separation of duties for key management. How does BYOK model look in practice?
36:07 Carlos: BYOK means you create keys in your cloud KMS or HSM and grant Redwood encryption/decryption permission via defined IAM roles. Keys never leave your KMS/HSM; all data-at-rest encryption uses those keys. We log key usage and can provide key usage reports for audits.

38:00 Anita: If we want on-prem, how do you handle network connectivity? Direct connect, VPN?
38:08 Priya: We support AWS Direct Connect, VPN, or in fully air-gapped scenarios we can do an offline package. Direct Connect is common for low-latency private links to our dedicated VPC.

40:00 Ethan: Time check — about 20 minutes left. Any particular deep dives needed?
40:06 Anita: I want to see example firewall rules and port matrix, plus the PrivateLink setup docs.
40:10 Priya: We'll share a doc with an example security group/NACL matrix and PrivateLink step-by-step.

42:00 David: Pen testing — do you allow external pen tests against the private environment?
42:07 Carlos: Yes, with a scope and schedule. For private deployments we coordinate and require approvals and a contact to avoid false positives on monitoring.

44:00 Michael: Incident response — if there's a suspected data exfil, how do we triage?
44:07 Priya: We have incident runbooks, playbooks for containment. We can dump flow logs, quarantine nodes by modifying security group to isolate, and escalate to your SOC via SLA. For severe incidents we have an on-call security engineer.

46:00 Sara: Are configuration changes logged to an immutable store?
46:05 Carlos: We can push config change logs to an append-only S3 bucket with MFA-delete enabled for immutability. We can also provide signed snapshots for auditor consumption.

48:00 Anita: Network egress labeling — can we tag flows for cost and audit?
48:06 Priya: Yes, we add metadata and tags to our telemetry and can provide structured logs with tenant and request IDs to correlate billing and security events.

50:00 David: For MFA, do you require hardware keys for admin ops?
50:06 Ethan: We support hardware MFA for critical roles; your identity provider (Okta, Azure AD) determines policy and we honor hardware MFA enforcement.

52:00 Michael: A question on rollback — if you deploy a model update, how quickly can we rollback and how is that controlled?
52:07 Priya: We have canary and rollback controls. Deploys are immutable images and we can rollback to prior version; we also provide audit trail for who initiated the rollout and the canary metrics.

54:00 Sara: For accreditation evidence, we'd like a single package with network diagrams, certs, IAM mappings, and key policies. Can you produce that?
54:06 Ethan: Yes, we'll package a compliance bundle for you — and we can redact parts if needed.

56:00 Priya: To summarize proposed secure topology: private subnets, PrivateLink for ingress, egress through transit VPC/appliances and strict egress whitelisting, BYOK via your KMS/HSM, audit logs forwarded to your SIEM, SSO via Okta with SCIM, RBAC separation, bastion for admin access, IDS/IPS integration.

57:20 Anita: That covers most. Couple quick clarifying Qs — what's the SLA for log delivery?
57:27 Carlos: Typically within 5-10 minutes for near real-time forwarding; archival deliveries to S3 may take longer depending on batch windows, but we can tune for near-real time.

58:30 Ethan: Next steps recap: we'll send SOC2/ISO certs, the PrivateLink step doc, and a sample firewall/port matrix. We'll set up a pilot VPC and schedule the packet-level walkthrough. Priya will send calendar invite for the walkthrough with networking folks.
58:55 Michael: Thanks everyone this was super helpful.
59:00 Sara: Thanks.
59:05 Ethan: Great, talk soon.
59:08 (call ends)
